passed.title: pl.from_epoch assumes seconds by default, so millisecond timestamps give wrong dates
passed.trap: `pl.from_epoch` defaults to `time_unit="s"`. JavaScript, Java and many APIs emit epoch values in milliseconds. Polars then reads those values as seconds, which gives dates tens of thousands of years in the future and raises no error. Always pass `time_unit` (`"ms"`, `"us"`, `"ns"` or `"d"`) to match your data. The unit also changes the output dtype: `"d"` returns `pl.Date`, and `"ms"` returns `Datetime("ms")`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"ts_ms": [1666683077000, 1666683099000]})

# Wrong: default time_unit="s" treats milliseconds as seconds
wrong = df.select(pl.from_epoch("ts_ms").dt.year().alias("year_with_default_s"))
print(wrong.to_series().to_list())

# Right: state the unit explicitly
right = df.select(pl.from_epoch("ts_ms", time_unit="ms").alias("ts"))
print(right.to_series().to_list())
print(right.schema)

passed.title: int_range excludes its end but datetime_range includes it, and both return an Expr by default
passed.trap: `pl.int_range` works like Python `range`, so `end` is exclusive. `pl.datetime_range` defaults to `closed="both"`, so `end` is included. Mixing the two leads to off-by-one row counts, so pass `closed="left"` to `pl.datetime_range` when you want a half-open range. Both functions default to `eager=False` and return a `pl.Expr`, not a `pl.Series`. Pass `eager=True` when you need a concrete `Series` outside a frame context.
passed.example:
import polars as pl
from datetime import datetime

print(isinstance(pl.int_range(0, 3), pl.Expr))  # True: Expr, not Series
print(pl.int_range(0, 3, eager=True).to_list())  # end excluded: [0, 1, 2]

start, end = datetime(2024, 1, 1), datetime(2024, 1, 3)
both = pl.datetime_range(start, end, "1d", eager=True)
left = pl.datetime_range(start, end, "1d", closed="left", eager=True)
print(both.len(), left.len())  # 3 (end included) vs 2

passed.title: pl.first and pl.last mean first column without arguments and first value with arguments
passed.trap: Called with no arguments, `pl.first()` and `pl.last()` select the first or last *column* of the context and keep every row. Called with column names, they return the first or last *value* of those columns, which is a single row. Adding or dropping an argument therefore changes the shape of the result completely. Write `pl.col(name).first()` when you want a value. Use `pl.first()` with no argument only when you mean positional column selection.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"a": [1, 8, 3], "b": [4, 5, 2]})

print(df.select(pl.first()).to_dict(as_series=False))      # first COLUMN 'a', 3 rows
print(df.select(pl.first("b")).to_dict(as_series=False))   # first VALUE of 'b', 1 row
print(df.select(pl.col("b").first()).to_dict(as_series=False))  # explicit equivalent
print(df.select(pl.last()).to_dict(as_series=False))       # last COLUMN 'b', 3 rows
print(df.select(pl.last("a")).to_dict(as_series=False))    # last VALUE of 'a' -> 3

passed.title: pl.duration is a fixed length with no months; use Expr.dt.offset_by for calendar shifts
passed.trap: `pl.duration` only accepts fixed units from `weeks` down to `nanoseconds`, so `days=1` means exactly 24 hours. It has no `months` or `years` parameter. Faking a month as `days=30` silently gives wrong dates. For calendar arithmetic such as months or years, use `Expr.dt.offset_by` with a duration string such as `"1mo"`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl
from datetime import datetime

df = pl.DataFrame({"dt": [datetime(2024, 1, 31), datetime(2024, 2, 29)]})

out = df.with_columns(
    plus_30d=pl.col("dt") + pl.duration(days=30),  # fixed: 2024-03-01, 2024-03-30
    plus_1mo=pl.col("dt").dt.offset_by("1mo"),     # calendar: 2024-02-29, 2024-03-29
)
for row in out.rows():
    print(row)

passed.title: pl.len counts rows including nulls, unlike a column count
passed.trap: `pl.len()` is the equivalent of SQL `COUNT(*)`: it counts the rows in the context, nulls included. `Expr.count` on a column counts only its non-null values. Swapping one for the other in a `DataFrame.group_by` aggregation silently gives wrong group sizes whenever nulls are present. Use `pl.len()` for row counts and `pl.col(...).count()` for non-null counts.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"g": ["x", "x", "y"], "v": [1, None, None]})

print(df.select(pl.len(), pl.col("v").count().alias("v_non_null")).to_dicts())
print(
    df.group_by("g", maintain_order=True)
    .agg(pl.len(), pl.col("v").count().alias("v_non_null"))
    .to_dicts()
)

passed.title: pl.groups is deprecated; collect row indices with with_row_index and group_by
passed.trap: `pl.groups` (sugar for `Expr.agg_groups`) is deprecated and slated for removal. Code that relies on it to get the row positions in each group will break when it is removed. The replacement is `DataFrame.with_row_index` followed by `DataFrame.group_by(...).agg(pl.col("index"))`. Pass `maintain_order=True` if you need the groups in first-appearance order.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"g": ["a", "b", "a"], "v": [10, 20, 30]})

# Replacement for the deprecated pl.groups("g")
out = (
    df.with_row_index()
    .group_by("g", maintain_order=True)
    .agg(pl.col("index"))
)
print(out.to_dicts())

passed.title: Use datetime_ranges, not datetime_range, for per-row ranges from columns
passed.trap: `pl.datetime_range` builds one range, so its `start` and `end` must each resolve to a single value. Passing multi-row columns raises an error. For one range per row, use `pl.datetime_ranges` (or `pl.int_ranges` for integers). These return a `List` column, not flat values. Call `DataFrame.explode` afterwards if you want one row per generated timestamp.
